overview: The law relating to contracts in India, governing agreement formation, enforceability, void agreements, performance, breach, and compensation.

sections.title: Contract Defined
sections.text: An agreement enforceable by law is a contract.
sections.explanation: Every promise and every set of promises, forming the consideration for each other, is an agreement. Only an agreement enforceable by law becomes a contract.

sections.chapter: Chapter II: Of Contracts, Voidable Contracts and Void Agreements
sections.title: What agreements are contracts
sections.text: All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void. Nothing herein contained shall affect any law in force in India, by which any contract is required to be made in writing or in the presence of witnesses, or any law relating to the registration of documents.
sections.explanation: An agreement must satisfy competency, free consent, lawful consideration, lawful purpose, and not be declared void by statute to be enforceable.

sections.chapter: Chapter II: Of Contracts, Voidable Contracts and Void Agreements
sections.title: Free consent defined
sections.text: Consent is said to be free when it is not caused by: (1) coercion, as defined in section 15, or (2) undue influence, as defined in section 16, or (3) fraud, as defined in section 17, or (4) misrepresentation, as defined in section 18, or (5) mistake, subject to the provisions of sections 20, 21 and 22. Consent is said to be so caused when it would not have been given but for the existence of such coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake.
sections.explanation: Consent obtained by force, pressure, deceit, or false statement makes the contract voidable at the option of the aggrieved party.

sections.chapter: Chapter II: Of Contracts, Voidable Contracts and Void Agreements
sections.title: Coercion defined
sections.text: 'Coercion' is the committing, or threatening to commit, any act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code (or Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita), or the unlawful detaining, or threatening to detain, any property, to the prejudice of any person whatever, with the intention of causing any person to enter into an agreement.
sections.explanation: Threatening criminal acts or illegally seizing property to force someone into signing an agreement constitutes coercion.

sections.chapter: Chapter II: Of Contracts, Voidable Contracts and Void Agreements
sections.title: Undue influence defined
sections.text: (1) A contract is said to be induced by 'undue influence' where the relations subsisting between the parties are such that one of the parties is in a position to dominate the will of the other and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage over the other. (2) In particular and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing principle, a person is deemed to be in a position to dominate the will of another: (a) where he holds a real or apparent authority over the other, or where he stands in a fiduciary relation to the other; or (b) where he makes a contract with a person whose mental capacity is temporarily or permanently affected by reason of age, illness, or mental or bodily distress.
sections.explanation: Occurs when an employer, landlord, or person with superior authority exploits their position to impose unfair terms.

sections.chapter: Chapter II: Of Contracts, Voidable Contracts and Void Agreements
sections.title: What considerations and objects are lawful, and what not
sections.text: The consideration or object of an agreement is lawful, unless: it is forbidden by law; or is of such a nature that, if permitted, it would defeat the provisions of any law; or is fraudulent; or involves or implies, injury to the person or property of another; or the Court regards it as immoral, or opposed to public policy. In each of these cases, the consideration or object of an agreement is said to be unlawful. Every agreement of which the object or consideration is unlawful is void.
sections.explanation: Agreements with illegal purpose, fraudulent motives, or those violating statutory enactments or public policy are void from the beginning (void ab initio).

sections.chapter: Chapter II: Of Contracts, Voidable Contracts and Void Agreements
sections.title: Agreement in restraint of trade, void
sections.text: Every agreement by which anyone is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind, is to that extent void. Exception 1: One who sells the goodwill of a business may agree with the buyer to refrain from carrying on a similar business, within specified local limits, so long as the buyer, or any person deriving title to the goodwill from him, carries on a like business therein, provided that such limits appear to the Court reasonable.
sections.explanation: Post-employment non-compete clauses restraining employees from working in the same industry after resignation/termination are generally void and unenforceable under Indian law (Percept D'Mark v Zaheer Khan, Niranjan Shankar Golikari).

sections.chapter: Chapter II: Of Contracts, Voidable Contracts and Void Agreements
sections.title: Agreements in restraint of legal proceedings, void
sections.text: Every agreement: (a) by which any party thereto is restricted absolutely from enforcing his rights under or in respect of any contract, by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals, or which limits the time within which he may thus enforce his rights; or (b) which extinguishes the rights of any party thereto, or discharges any party thereto, from any liability, under or in respect of any contract on the expiry of a specified period so as to restrict any party from enforcing his rights, is void to that extent. Exception 1 & 2 save arbitration clauses.
sections.explanation: Clauses barring a party from approaching court or shortening the statutory limitation period (usually 3 years for contract claims) are void.

sections.chapter: Chapter IV: Of the Performance of Contracts
sections.title: Effect of refusal of party to perform promise wholly
sections.text: When a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified, by words or conduct, his acquiescence in its continuance.
sections.explanation: Anticipatory breach: if one party explicitly refuses to perform before the due date, the other party has the right to terminate the contract immediately and claim damages.

sections.chapter: Chapter IV: Of the Performance of Contracts
sections.title: Agreement to do impossible act (Doctrine of Frustration)
sections.text: An agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void. Contract to do act afterwards becoming impossible or unlawful: A contract to do an act which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible, or, by reason of some event which the promisor could not prevent, unlawful, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful.
sections.explanation: Supervening impossibility or frustration discharges both parties from performance if the event was unexpected and beyond their control (e.g. government ban, destruction of subject matter).

sections.chapter: Chapter VI: Of the Consequences of Breach of Contract
sections.title: Compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract
sections.text: When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach.
sections.explanation: The fundamental remedy for contract breach is damages for direct, natural loss suffered. Indirect or remote losses cannot be recovered unless specifically contemplated.

sections.chapter: Chapter VI: Of the Consequences of Breach of Contract
sections.title: Compensation for breach of contract where penalty stipulated for
sections.text: When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.
sections.explanation: Indian courts do not enforce disproportionate penalties. Only reasonable compensation up to the stipulated maximum (liquidated damages) is awarded upon proof of injury (Fateh Chand v Balkishan Das, Kailash Nath Associates v DDA).
